title: GracePeriod abstraction for host eviction and throughput contracts
creator: Arjun Patel
description:
Background: Dedicated fleets need clear, machine-enforceable contracts that bind eviction behavior to throughput guarantees and rolling windows. Current implementations use ad-hoc drain timers per controller, which causes customer-visible throughput blips when capacity is reclaimed or nodes are patched. This ticket introduces a GracePeriod abstraction and eviction-contract primitives to coordinate drains, backfills, and autoscaler decisions across the fleet while respecting per-tenant throughput reservations.

Goals:
- Define a system-level GracePeriod API that exposes (duration, priority, allowed-reduction-percent, preemptibility) and can be attached to any host eviction event.
- Ensure autoscaling decisions and rolling upgrade controllers consult GracePeriod to avoid violating throughput contracts (quota-backed SLA).
- Implement a coordinator that schedules staggered drains based on tenant-level throughput reservations and runtime KPIs (tail-latency, active-connections, KV-cache-hit-rate).
- Provide tracing and dashboarding hooks to show how a given eviction affected throughput and which throttles were applied.

Non-goals:
- Replacing customer-facing billing/commit logic (this ticket assumes reservation metadata from Dedicated provisioning exists).
- Deep changes to the runtime scheduler kernel selection — we interact via high-level capacity signals only.

Design decisions so far:
- Use a central lightweight coordinator service (stateless, leader-elected per region) to sequence eviction windows; controllers continue to own node-level drain implementation. This avoids complex distributed consensus across controllers.
- GracePeriod is modeled as an immutable token issued for each planned maintenance epoch; controllers accept tokens and must report progress. Tokens carry semantic fields (requestor, start_ts, end_ts, min_throughput_pct, rollback_policy).
- To minimize customer impact, eviction windows for tenants with throughput reservations are prioritized at the end of a maintenance epoch; low-priority tenants get earlier drains or preemption.

Trade-offs discussed in design review:
- Central coordinator vs. fully decentralized CRDT approach: chose central coordinator for simplicity and observability; potential single-region leader failure mitigated with fast leader failover.
- Conservative min_throughput_pct vs. optimistic best-effort: we default to conservative (90%) for first rollout. Tight guarantees add complexity to autoscaler heuristics; we plan to relax in future iterations after telemetry analysis.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) API surface and token schema proposal + design doc (this ticket) — complete.
2) Coordinator service prototype (leader election, token issuance, status API) — in progress.
3) Controller contract update (accept token, report step) and staged rollout to canary fleet.
4) Autoscaler integration: consult token and delay scale-downs when min_throughput_pct would be violated.
5) Console and traces: dashboard tile for eviction token lifecycle and per-tenant throughput deltas.

Acceptance criteria:
- Coordinator issues tokens and controllers accept/ack via API.
- Canary rollout shows <5% deviation from pre-maintenance throughput for tenants with reservations during a controlled drain (first 2 canaries).
- Autoscaler respects token-specified hold windows and no regressions in cost per token.

- Coordinator prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/fleet-coordinator/pull/412
- Controller changes PR (draft): https://github.com/redwood-inference/node-controller/pull/1198
- Dashboard mockups: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1aGracePeriodDashMock

Next steps:
- Complete coordinator leader-election and token-issuance endpoints (due 2026-03-20).
- Add unit tests for token validation and controller acceptance handshake.
- Schedule cross-team demo with Autoscaler and Console owners (Mar 18).
